corrections.was: Karel Čapek's play stages artificial workers who rebel, and hands the language a name for the anxiety.
corrections.now: Karel Čapek's play, published in 1920, stages artificial workers who rebel. Its word for them, robot, was his brother Josef's, Karel wrote in 1933.
corrections.why: The word was not Karel Čapek's own, by his account in Lidové noviny on 24 December 1933: he had thought of calling the artificial workers laboři, and his brother Josef, painting with a brush in his mouth, told him to call them roboti. That it handed the language a name for an anxiety had no source, and the fear it came to carry, of machines taking people's place, is one the author disowned in 1935. The play was in print in 1920 and first staged in January 1921. Čapek's own words of 1935, that his robots were not mechanisms but were made by a chemical path, now stand in the card's reading.

source.title: O slově robot (Karel Čapek)

corrections.was: Fritz Lang's Maschinenmensch fixes the humanoid machine in the visual imagination for a century.
corrections.now: Fritz Lang's film of Thea von Harbou's novel premieres in Berlin. Its Maschinenmensch, a steel robot given the likeness of the workers' leader Maria, is the work of the sculptor Walter Schulze-Mittendorff.
corrections.why: The machine-man was not Lang's alone. The film is based on Thea von Harbou's novel of 1925, in which Fredersen orders machine-men from the inventor Rotwang, and she wrote the screenplay, with Lang uncredited; the figure itself was made by the sculptor Walter Schulze-Mittendorff, whose biography on the German film institute's filmportal says he created the Machine Man Maria. That it fixed the humanoid machine in the imagination for a century had no source, and a century has not yet passed since the premiere; an attributed reading now stands in the card's why.

corrections.was: The first hard limit on formal reasoning, and the opening move in a debate about machine minds that never closed.
corrections.now: It limits what any one formal system can prove. Turing, in 1950, answered the objection that it and results like it show machines to be limited in a way people are not; J. R. Lucas argued in 1961 that it proves minds cannot be explained as machines.
corrections.why: No source made the theorems the first limit on formal reasoning, and the debate about machine minds did not open with them: the paper of 1950 in which Turing answers the objection drawn from Gödel's theorem also answers Lady Lovelace's, from her memoir of 1842, and Gödel's paper itself says nothing of minds or machines. Turing weighed the argument from the late 1940s, by the Stanford Encyclopedia's account, and answered it in 1950; Lucas pressed it in 1961. That the debate never closed had no source.

corrections.was: set the limit Turing extended in
corrections.now: ruled out a quick answer to the problem settled in
corrections.why: Turing did not present his result as an extension of Gödel's. His paper calls its conclusions superficially similar to Gödel's and what it proves quite different; the link it draws is that, had the negation of Gödel's result been proved, the Entscheidungsproblem would have had an immediate solution. Gödel, for his part, later credited Turing's definition of a formal system with making his theorems fully general, the Stanford Encyclopedia records.

corrections.was: The result is the fence around everything a machine can be asked to decide.
corrections.now: The limit on what a machine can decide is Turing's, of 1936, which he called quite different from Gödel's results.
corrections.why: The fence around what a machine can decide is Turing's, on the board's own record and on Turing's: his paper of 1936 calls what it proves quite different from the well-known results of Gödel, and in 1950 he wrote that his result refers directly to machines, while the others can be used only in a comparatively indirect argument. Gödel's theorems limit what a formal system can prove.

corrections.was: the programme — to put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — that Gödel and Turing answered in the negative.
corrections.now: the programme — to put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — that Gödel's theorems are generally taken to rule out, and whose decision problem Turing answered in the negative.
corrections.why: Gödel did not answer the programme in the negative in 1931: his paper notes expressly that its theorem on consistency proofs is no contradiction of Hilbert's formalistic standpoint, since finitary proofs that cannot be stated in his system are conceivable. He came to hold, after Turing's definition of a formal system, that the theorems refuted the programme; that they are generally taken to show it cannot be carried out is the Stanford Encyclopedia's reading, which Hilbert's card already gives. Turing answered the programme's decision problem, not the programme.

corrections.was: Claude Shannon's master's thesis shows electrical relays can compute logic.
corrections.now: Claude Shannon's master's thesis at MIT shows that Boolean algebra describes relay and switching circuits, so that a circuit can be analysed, or designed to order, by calculation.
corrections.why: The thesis gives relay circuits an algebra. That relays could carry out logical operations was not its result: they already did, in automatic telephone exchanges and industrial motor controls, as its first paragraph says, and the thesis mentions using circuits to represent logical relations only as the analogy run the other way, with results it calls of no importance there. Its result is a calculus, shown to be exactly analogous to the calculus of propositions, in which each circuit is written as equations, used both to analyse a given circuit and to find a circuit with given characteristics. N. J. A. Sloane and A. D. Wyner, editors of his collected papers, sum the thesis up as Boolean algebra used in the analysis and synthesis of switching circuits.

source.publisher: Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, vol. 57 (course copy, Iowa State University)
source.title: A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits (Claude E. Shannon)

corrections.was: Thought becomes wiring — the bridge from mathematics to hardware.
corrections.now: The analogy runs both ways: a circuit can be checked and simplified as algebra, and any operation that can be described in a finite number of steps with the words 'if', 'or' and 'and', Shannon writes, can be done automatically with relays. Others found the link independently in the Soviet Union and in Japan, Toma Kawanishi records, but Shannon's work overshadowed theirs.
corrections.why: Shannon's was not the only bridge. Research linking relay circuits to Boolean algebra began independently in the 1930s in the United States, with Shannon, in the Soviet Union, with Viktor Shestakov, and in Japan, with Akira Nakashima of NEC and his colleague Masao Hanzawa, the historian Toma Kawanishi writes, though Shannon has overshadowed the others. What the thesis itself says of the hardware side is that any operation that can be completely described in a finite number of steps with if, or and and can be done automatically with relays.

source.publisher: Historia Scientiarum, History of Science Society of Japan (J-STAGE)

corrections.was: turned logic into the circuits of
corrections.now: gave circuit design an algebra before
corrections.why: Nothing on the record ties Shannon's thesis to the EDVAC. Von Neumann's report of 1945 builds its logic from idealised neurons and cites McCulloch and Pitts for them; besides them it names only Aiken, Stibitz and Mauchly, for a multiplication scheme, an arithmetic trick and a rounding rule. Shannon is not in it, and Eckert's, Goldstine's and Warren's accounts of the work do not connect him to it. What the record does show is the order: Shannon's algebra of switching circuits is dated 1937, eight years before the report.

corrections.was: A brain cell is modelled as a logical threshold unit: the first claim that thinking might be computable.
corrections.now: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts treat nerve cells as all-or-none units with thresholds, show that their nets realise logical expressions, and argue that an organism can compute just what a Turing machine can.
corrections.why: The paper does not claim to be the first to make thinking computable. It offers itself as a psychological justification of Turing's definition of computability, published in 1936 and on the board, and argues that any number an organism can compute is computable by that definition, and conversely. What it does claim is that nets of all-or-none neurons, each fired only when enough of its synapses are excited at once, can be described in propositional logic, and that for any logical expression meeting certain conditions a net can be found that behaves as it describes.

corrections.was: Everything called a neural network descends from this abstraction.
corrections.now: The Nobel committee called it in 2024 a launch pad for later research into neural networks, biological and artificial.
corrections.why: Nothing on the record says that everything called a neural network descends from the paper. Rosenblatt, whose perceptron the board strings to it, counted McCulloch and Pitts in 1958 among the authors of brain models that were logical contrivances, and built his own in probability theory on the position of Hebb and Hayek. The Nobel committee's background of 2024 says what the record bears out: their work became a launch pad for later research into both biological and artificial neural networks. The register's entry of 11 September 2026, which took out the two pages, is untouched: the paper's length is not stated.

corrections.why: The perceptron was not built of McCulloch and Pitts's neurons. Rosenblatt's paper of 1958 lists their model among brain models that amount to logical contrivances for particular algorithms, and says that analysing systems whose precise structure is unknown led him to formulate his own in terms of probability theory rather than symbolic logic. His units do fire, as theirs do, all or nothing once their summed input reaches a threshold; but the Mark I's hardware, by the perceptron card's own figures, was photocells and weights turned by motors.

corrections.now: With Walter Pitts, modelled the nerve cell as a logic gate in 1943 — a launch pad, the Nobel committee wrote in 2024, for later research into neural networks, biological and artificial.
corrections.why: No primary on the record makes the 1943 paper the first neural network on paper: Rosenblatt in 1958 put it in a list of brain models of the same logical kind that begins with Rashevsky's book of 1938, and the Nobel committee's background of 2024 says only that McCulloch and Pitts proposed their model as early as 1943, and that their work became a launch pad for later research into biological and artificial neural networks, which the file now says. corrections.why: The 1943 paper models nets of neurons, not the single cell: the Nobel committee calls it a model for how the neurons in the brain cooperate. That it was the first neural network is in no primary on the record, and the first goes, as on McCulloch's file.

corrections.was: Von Neumann's EDVAC report describes machines that hold instructions in the same memory as data.
corrections.now: Von Neumann's draft report on the EDVAC has the machine take its orders from the memory that holds its numbers. Eckert said von Neumann more or less claimed the team's work as his own; Goldstine credited von Neumann.
corrections.why: The report is von Neumann's; whose ideas it set down is disputed, and the card gave them to him alone. J. Presper Eckert, co-inventor of the ENIAC with John Mauchly, told the Charles Babbage Institute in 1977 that von Neumann grasped what they were doing quite quickly and then more or less claimed it as his own. The report names Mauchly once, for a rounding rule, and Eckert not at all, and S. Reid Warren, the Moore School's supervisor of the EDVAC project, agreed that putting it out without proper acknowledgement was unethical. Herman Goldstine said in 1980 that in his mind von Neumann invented the stored program, owing Turing a debt he could not measure. The report describes one machine, the EDVAC, whose control takes its orders from the same place where the numbers are stored.

corrections.was: Neurons that fire together wire together — Donald Hebb gives learning a physical mechanism.
corrections.now: Donald Hebb postulates that when one nerve cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, some growth or metabolic change makes it better at doing so. The slogan “cells that fire together wire together” came in 1992.
corrections.why: The slogan is not Hebb's. Stanford's magazine credits Carla Shatz with coining it, and she printed it in Scientific American in September 1992; Siegrid Löwel and Wolf Singer wrote in Science the same year that neurons wire together if they fire together. Hebb's own words, in The Organization of Behavior, are a postulate: when an axon of cell A repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing cell B, some growth process or metabolic change makes A more efficient as one of the cells firing B. He put it forward as an assumption, under the heading of a neurophysiological postulate, and the Nobel committee writes that he proposed a mechanism for learning and memories.

source.title: The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory (D. O. Hebb)

corrections.was: Every learning rule on the board, backpropagation included, is a formalisation of the idea.
corrections.now: Rumelhart, Hinton and McClelland wrote in 1986 that virtually all learning rules for networks like theirs, the delta rule among them, could be considered variants of his rule.
corrections.why: Not every learning rule on the board formalises Hebb's postulate: the board's reinforcement learners learn from a reward, and backpropagation from an error, neither of which the postulate mentions. The authors of backpropagation claimed less in the second chapter of Parallel Distributed Processing: virtually all learning rules for models of their type can be considered a variant of Hebb's, among them the delta rule, which learns from the difference between the activation a unit reaches and the target a teacher gives.

corrections.was: SNARC, the first neural net machine
corrections.now: SNARC, a learning machine of forty neurons
corrections.why: No primary on the record makes SNARC the first neural-net machine. Minsky's own biography claims a narrower first, the first randomly wired neural network learning machine; Jeremy Bernstein, who interviewed Minsky for The New Yorker in 1981, called it one of the first electronic learning machines, and perhaps the very first; the MIT Media Lab's memorial page calls it the first neural network simulator. The title now says what Minsky said it was, forty neurons that learned, and the card's reading carries the firsts, attributed. The register's entry of 20 October 2026 (minsky-snarc-one-of-the-first) took the same first out of Minsky's file; the card now follows it. The id keeps its old words.

corrections.was: Minsky and Edmonds wire 3,000 vacuum tubes into a machine that learns to run a maze.
corrections.now: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds, graduate students at Princeton, build at Harvard a machine of about three hundred vacuum tubes in which a simulated rat learns its way through a maze.
corrections.why: Minsky told Jeremy Bernstein in 1981 that the machine had three hundred tubes, nearly three hundred with the thousands of connections soldered, from a design of six tubes and a motor for each of its forty neurons: not three thousand. He and Edmonds, graduate students at Princeton in mathematics and in physics, built it at Harvard in the summer of 1951. The machine did not itself run a maze: a simulated rat, made of its forty neurons, learned a path through a copy of a maze Claude Shannon had built, as Minsky told Web of Stories in 2011.

corrections.why: MIT had no part in SNARC. Minsky and Edmonds were graduate students at Princeton who built it at Harvard in the summer of 1951, with money George Miller of Harvard found; Minsky and McCarthy set up their group at MIT in 1958, Bernstein records. The board has no file for Harvard or Princeton, and the summary now names both. The field goes.

The Office of Naval Research's newsletter of July 1960 reports that the Mark I was demonstrated publicly for the first time in June, at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. corrections.was: At its 1958 press conference the Navy said it expected the machine to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence, and the newspapers printed it.
corrections.now: At the Navy's press conference of July 1958, before the Mark I was built, the perceptron ran as a simulation on an IBM 704, and a United Press International report in The New York Times said the Navy expected the machine to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. Rosenblatt himself wrote that summer that a perceptron could in principle read print and script and respond to spoken commands, and later blamed the popular press, which he said fell to the task with the discretion of a pack of happy bloodhounds.
corrections.why: The press conference was not the Mark I's: in July 1958 the machine was still being designed, and Rosenblatt demonstrated the perceptron as a simulation on a digital computer, an IBM 704, as Mikel Olazaran's history records from the reports of the day. The expectation that it would walk and talk is the Navy's as United Press International reported it; the board has no text of the Navy's own statement. Nor was the overclaim the Navy's and the newspapers' alone: Rosenblatt's own article in his laboratory's magazine, Research Trends, that summer says the perceptron can in principle read print and script and respond to verbal commands, and in 1961 he blamed the popular press for its handling of the first announcement.

corrections.was: John McCarthy's language treats code as data and becomes the lingua franca of AI research for thirty years.
corrections.now: John McCarthy's list-processing language, implemented at MIT from 1958, writes its programs as lists, the data it computes with. By the mid-1980s, Guy Steele and Richard Gabriel write, it was the language of AI.
corrections.why: No source on the record gives Lisp thirty years as the lingua franca of AI research. Guy Steele and Richard Gabriel, in their history of Lisp for the second History of Programming Languages conference, write that when Common Lisp was published, in 1984, AI was on the rise and Lisp was the language of AI; the same paper names Lisp and Prolog as the two perhaps foremost families of AI programming languages. That Lisp's programs are its own data stands, in McCarthy's account: the notation for LISP functions as LISP data was invented to write eval for his paper of 1960, with no thought that programs would be written in it, and S. R. Russell then hand-coded eval as the interpreter. The implementation began at MIT in the autumn of 1958.

corrections.now: A Unimate arm, which the International Federation of Robotics calls the first industrial robot, starts work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey, taking hot metal parts from a die-casting machine.
corrections.why: The first is an attribution, not a fact the record settles. The International Federation of Robotics and IEEE Spectrum's robot guide call the Unimate the first industrial robot, and The Henry Ford, which holds a Unimate it says was the first installed, says that Unimate made the first successful industrial robots; Assembly magazine, on the fiftieth anniversary, said the Unimate was not the first robot to hit the market, AMF's Versatran having been developed a year earlier. corrections.was: Automation of the body arrives sixty years before automation of the desk, and the labour debate rhymes.
corrections.now: Automation of the arm reaches the factory floor as the computer reaches the office desk, and the argument about jobs arrives with both. It rhymes with today's.
corrections.why: Automation of the desk did not wait sixty years. corrections.was: Andrey Markov models sequences where the next state depends only on the present one, using the letters of a Pushkin poem.
corrections.now: Andrey Markov tests the chains he had worked out in theory since 1906 on the first 20,000 letters of Pushkin's novel in verse Eugene Onegin, and finds that whether a letter is a vowel depends on the letters before it.
corrections.why: Markov's paper of 1913, in its English translation, counts 20,000 letters of Pushkin's novel as vowels and consonants and measures how a vowel depends on the letter before it and on the two before it, not on one alone. The chains themselves date from 1906, David Link writes; 1913 was the first time Markov tried them on a text, which he calls a novel.

corrections.was: Every language model is, at bottom, a very large next-token probability.
corrections.now: A large language model gives, at bottom, the probability of the next token given the ones before it. Markov asked that of Pushkin's vowels and consonants, one letter and two letters back.
corrections.why: Not every language model predicts the next token; the board's glossary defines the large ones as models that do, and the card now says so. That the framing starts with Markov stays the board's reading; David Link calls him the first to develop a complete theory of the connections between letters.

corrections.was: Shannon approximated written English as a Markov process — letters, then words, each drawn from the frequencies of what came before — and printed the results.
corrections.now: Shannon approximated written English as what he called a discrete Markoff process and printed the results: letters, then words, picked first by chance alone, then by their frequencies, then by what usually followed the letters or word before.
corrections.why: Not every step in Shannon's series drew on what came before. His section 3 picks the first letters independently and with equal chances, the next independently with the frequencies of English, and the first words independently with theirs; only the digram, trigram and word-transition steps depend on what precedes.

source.publisher: Bell System Technical Journal (scan, Internet Archive)

corrections.was: It is the first statistical language model; the next-token framing begins here.
corrections.now: Markov had counted how a letter depends on the one before; Shannon, in David Link's account, was the first to use the method to generate text rather than to analyse it.
corrections.why: Nothing on the record made Shannon's series the first statistical language model, and the string's other end, Markov's count of 1913, is itself a statistical model of a text's letters; the note also started the next-token framing here while Markov's card starts it there. David Link's account, that Shannon was the first to use Markov's method to generate text rather than to analyse it, stands in its place.

corrections.was: Shannon defines the bit and gives information a unit of measure.
corrections.now: Claude Shannon measures information in bits, a word he credits to John Tukey, generalising the logarithmic measure Ralph Hartley set out in 1928, and works out how much a noisy channel can carry.
corrections.why: Information had a measure and a unit before 1948: Ralph Hartley's paper of 1928 sets out a logarithmic measure and notes that the base chosen fixes the size of the unit of information. Shannon credits the logarithm to Hartley, generalises it, and says the word bits was suggested by J. W. Tukey. Shannon's file and the blurb of finding 2 had given him the unit too.

corrections.was: Compression, prediction and learning turn out to be the same problem seen from different angles.
corrections.now: Shannon's measure makes compression and prediction one problem: the better the next letter can be guessed, the fewer bits it takes to send. A language model is trained to make that guess.
corrections.why: Compression and prediction are tied on the record: Shannon's paper makes entropy the limit of compression, his paper of 1951 estimates it from people's guesses at the next letter, and that predictors and lossless compressors convert into each other is long established, as Delétang and colleagues put it. That learning is the same problem is a view, not a result.

corrections.why: The note gave HAL's motive as fact. In the film it is HAL's own account, that the mission is too important to let Bowman jeopardise it, and his motives are otherwise left open; Kubrick and Clarke's screenplay of 1965 explains him by a conflict between his truth programming and orders to lie, with disconnection, which must have seemed the equivalent of death, as the last straw.

corrections.was: Minsky and Papert prove the single-layer limit; funding for neural approaches evaporates for a decade.
corrections.now: Minsky and Papert prove that perceptrons built from local detectors cannot tell an odd number of dots from an even one, or a connected figure from a broken one. A hiatus in neural-network funding follows.
corrections.why: The book's theorems are about perceptrons whose units each see a limited part of the picture: such machines cannot compute parity or, Minsky and Papert wrote in 1972, define connectedness. That funding evaporated for a decade is the popular telling, which the sociologist Mikel Olazaran argues against; the Nobel committee's background of 2024 says the book led to a hiatus in neural-network funding, and the card says that much. The blurb of finding 5 now speaks of a book of proofs, not one result.

corrections.was: A correct proof about a narrow case, generalised into a field-wide dismissal. Depth was the answer all along.
corrections.now: Correct proofs about one kind of machine, read as a verdict on all neural networks, and the authors helped: they judged, by intuition, that the many-layered extension was sterile. In 1986 networks with hidden layers were trained to do what one layer could not. Two years later the authors replied that progress had stalled before their book appeared.
corrections.why: Part of the generalising was the book's own: Minsky and Papert called it their intuitive judgement that the many-layered extension is sterile, the passage Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams quoted in 1986 before training networks with hidden layers. What had been missing was a way to train more than one layer, not depth. The glossary's entry on the perceptron now says the same.

corrections.now: had its limits proved by
corrections.why: The book did not disprove the perceptron. It proved what perceptrons of limited reach cannot compute, and Minsky and Papert's own summary of 1972 calls their learning effective within the concepts they can represent.

corrections.was: A narrow mathematical result about single-layer networks was read as a verdict on the whole approach. Funders believed it, and the money left for a decade.
corrections.now: Proofs about perceptrons built from local detectors were read, by researchers and funders alike, as a verdict on neural networks as a whole, and a hiatus in their funding followed, though the authors said progress had stalled already. The slowdown of the mid-1970s then fell hardest on the symbolic laboratories that had won the argument.
corrections.why: Both authors admitted that researchers and people in the funding agencies linked the book to rejecting neural networks, Mikel Olazaran records; but that the money left because of it is the popular account he argues against, finding Rosenblatt already short of support in the mid-1960s. Nor did the book freeze the funding of the 1970s, as the string's claim had it: that slowdown fell on DARPA's symbolic laboratories.

corrections.now: DARPA's money for AI must now serve a military purpose and comes with demands for results, and in Britain Lighthill's report costs the field its standing. Promises had outrun results.
corrections.why: DARPA's money did not simply stop. The National Research Council's history says its flow to Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Stanford did not cease or even diminish much, but came with demands for interim reports and results, after a law of 1969 tied Pentagon research money to military use. Lost credibility was chiefly Britain's, after the Lighthill report. DARPA's and Lighthill's files and the glossary said funding collapsed or stopped.

corrections.was: The work continued quietly under other names.
corrections.now: What slowdown there was fell on a few elite laboratories, whose DARPA money came with strings but did not stop, while the ACM's AI group, SIGART, nearly tripled its membership between 1973 and 1978. The historian Thomas Haigh argues there was no first winter at all.

corrections.now: Japan's trade ministry starts a ten-year programme to build parallel computers that process knowledge through logic programming. America, Britain and the European Community answer with programmes of their own.
corrections.why: ICOT's aim, as its directors put it in 1992, was new computer systems combining highly parallel processing with knowledge information processing in logic programming, not intelligent machines in general. The answers abroad are credited to it by the National Research Council for DARPA and by ICOT's evaluators for Alvey and ESPRIT; America's MCC was private money.

corrections.now: A ministry's bet on logic programming set other governments racing over the computers of the future; some, one evaluator recalled, spoke even of a technological war. It closed in 1992 having, by ICOT's account, achieved its initial goal; the New York Times reported it fizzling to a close, short of many of its goals.
corrections.why: Neither first had a source, and the end was neither quiet nor agreed: ICOT told the National Science Foundation that the project concluded in 1992 after achieving its initial goal, while the New York Times reported that it had failed to meet many of its goals. The string to the chip controls had it ending in quiet disappointment too.

corrections.was: The 1982 race was over software and ended in quiet disappointment. The 2022 one is over silicon, and is fought with customs law rather than research grants.
corrections.now: The 1982 race was over a new kind of computer, hardware and software together, and ended in dispute: ICOT said it had reached its initial goal, the press that it had fallen short. The 2022 one is over silicon, and is fought with export licences rather than research grants.
corrections.why: The Fifth Generation project built parallel inference machines as well as their software, and its end was contested, not quiet. The 2022 controls work by export licence, as the board's card on them says, not by customs law. Nor was it the last state AI race before them, as the string's claim had it: China's State Council set out its own plan in 2017.

corrections.was: A physicist's model of associative memory brings statistical mechanics into neural computation.
corrections.now: John Hopfield, a physicist, describes a network that stores memories as the low points of an energy taken from the physics of magnets, and recalls a whole memory from part of it.
corrections.why: Hopfield's paper of 1982 makes the network isomorphic with an Ising model of magnetism and has it settle into a minimum of that energy. It did not bring that physics into neural computation: the Nobel committee's background lists models of neural networks inspired by magnetic systems from 1955, and Hopfield's paper cites William Little's of 1974.

corrections.why: The prize went to Hopfield, shared with Geoffrey Hinton, not to the network. The Nobel committee describes the Boltzmann machine, which Hinton developed with Terrence Sejnowski and others between 1983 and 1985, as a stochastic extension of Hopfield's model; the string to the Nobel card had Hinton building it alone.

corrections.why: The Nobel committee's popular account says interest in neural networks was reawakened in the 1980s when several important ideas made an impact; Hopfield's network was one of them, not the whole revival.

corrections.was: LeCun's network learns digits from raw pixels and reads handwritten US Postal Service zip codes.
corrections.now: LeCun and colleagues at Bell Labs train a network by backpropagation to read handwritten digits cut from zip codes on US mail, feeding it the pixels of each normalised image rather than hand-designed features.
corrections.why: The network read single digits, which Postal Service contractors had already located and cut from the zip codes and which were scaled to 16 by 16 pixels before it saw them, as the companion NIPS paper describes: neither whole zip codes nor raw pixels. The string to Facebook's hiring of LeCun said it read zip codes too.

corrections.was: The first deep learning system in production, running at national scale before the term existed.
corrections.now: One of the first demonstrations, LeCun writes, that neural networks could do real-world work. Its descendant LeNet-5 read millions of cheques a day in American banks from 1996: by LeCun's account, an estimated tenth of all the cheques written in the US.
corrections.why: No source puts the 1989 network in production: its makers ran it on a signal-processing board in a PC. corrections.why: Midjourney opened its beta on 12 July 2022, OpenAI began inviting a million people to DALL·E on 20 July and Stable Diffusion went to the public on 22 August: weeks apart, not months. Its weights were open to anyone who clicked to accept the CreativeML OpenRAIL-M licence on Hugging Face, which bars harmful uses.

corrections.was: Both the leaked Google memo and Simon Willison called it the "Stable Diffusion moment" for language models: an open base model, then a flood of community fine-tunes, quantisation and local inference within weeks. The difference is that Stability chose to release and Meta did not.
corrections.now: Simon Willison called it the "Stable Diffusion moment" for language models, and the leaked Google memo said many were calling it that: a capable base model loose, then a flood of community fine-tunes, quantisation and local inference within weeks. The difference is that Stability released its weights to anyone who accepted a licence, while Meta gave LLaMA's to approved researchers, and they leaked.
corrections.why: The memo did not use the phrase as its own: it said many were calling it the Stable Diffusion moment, as Simon Willison had in March 2023. And Meta did release LLaMA, to researchers granted access case by case, before the weights leaked.

corrections.now: Stable Diffusion's weights sat behind a one-click licence on Hugging Face that barred harmful uses, and a community built on them. Mistral went further: no form, no restrictions under its Apache 2.0 licence, a torrent.
corrections.why: Stable Diffusion's first public weights were gated: Hugging Face asked users to share their contact details and accept the CreativeML OpenRAIL-M licence before granting access. Nothing on the record compares the community it built with any API's.

Microsoft told The Verge it began testing a chat feature of that name in India in late 2020, and The Verge found rude replies from a Sydney bot posted on Microsoft's forums in November 2022. corrections.was: David Hilbert asks whether all of mathematics can be mechanised — question ten becomes the seed of computability.
corrections.now: David Hilbert sets out twenty-three problems for the new century. The tenth asks for a process that decides, by a finite number of operations, whether an equation has whole-number solutions.
corrections.why: Hilbert's address, in the Bulletin's translation of 1902, asks for no machine: problem ten asks for a process for one kind of equation, and the methods to show none exists came later, Martin Davis writes. The programme for all of mathematics dates from the early 1920s, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records, and Hilbert's file now says so.

corrections.was: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Turing and Gödel later prove impossible, and in failing, invent computing.
corrections.now: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Gödel and Turing later take apart — Gödel the programme, Turing the procedure — and to take it apart Turing has to define computing.
corrections.why: Gödel's work of 1931 bears on Hilbert's programme. That no decision procedure exists is what Turing showed, in his paper of 1936, which says the Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution; the card had credited Gödel with it too.

corrections.was: Paris, 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians
corrections.now: Paris, 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians: ten aloud, all twenty-three in print
corrections.why: Hilbert read ten of the problems in Paris, the tenth not among them by Wikipedia's list, and printed all twenty-three afterwards, as the card's own file says. Charlotte Angas Scott, reporting from the congress, called those he mentioned a selection from a much longer list.

corrections.was: The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether any polynomial equation has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was stated most sharply in 1928 as the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide any mathematical statement.
corrections.now: The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was joined in 1928 by its sharpest question, the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide whether any statement of logic is provable.
corrections.why: Problem ten is for equations with whole-number coefficients, in the Bulletin's translation, and the Entscheidungsproblem, as Turing's paper sets it out, asks for a process to decide whether a formula of logic is provable, not any mathematical statement. The string to Turing's card now says so too.

corrections.was: Gödel showed in 1931 that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it.
corrections.now: Gödel's theorems of 1931 are generally taken to show that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it.
corrections.why: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, now on the card, gives this as a reading: Gödel's work, it says, is generally taken to show that Hilbert's programme cannot be carried out. The card had said Gödel showed it.

source.title: Hilbert’s Program

corrections.was: The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 by Yuri Matiyasevich, the same way: no such procedure.
corrections.now: The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 the same way — no such procedure — when Yuri Matiyasevich completed a decade of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson.
corrections.why: The result was not Matiyasevich's alone. Martin Davis, one of the four, writes that when Matiyasevich announced his solution in January 1970, it had been known for a decade that the problem's unsolvability would follow from one construction, which Matiyasevich found.

corrections.now: The same idea later produces AlphaGo and, in a looser sense, the reinforcement fine-tuning of today's models.
corrections.why: Samuel's program learned partly from games against itself. By the board's own glossary, today's models are fine-tuned on raters' preferences, and the reasoning models play themselves only in a sense, against problems with checkable answers.

corrections.was: It is the first program to get better at something without being told how, and the word he used for it — machine learning — is the field's name for the technique ever since.
corrections.now: It is one of the first programs to get better at something without being told how, and the word he used for it — machine learning — is the field's name for the technique ever since.

corrections.was: First general-purpose programming platform on a graphics card
corrections.now: First C compiler for a graphics chip, as Nvidia billed it

corrections.was: A graphics card is thousands of small processors doing the same arithmetic on different pixels.

corrections.was: Nvidia built it for scientific computing and games; the researchers who trained networks on it in 2009–2012 were the customers nobody planned for, and after AlexNet they were the only customers that mattered.
corrections.now: Nvidia built it for scientific computing and games; the researchers who trained networks on it in 2009–2012 were the customers nobody planned for, and ten years after AlexNet Nvidia was selling more to datacentres than to gamers.
corrections.why: Gamers were still Nvidia's larger market nearly a decade after AlexNet. Its results of February 2023 put data-centre revenue for the year at $15.01 billion, up 41%, and gaming at $9.07 billion, down 27%, which makes gaming the larger of the two the year before.

corrections.was: Open-domain question answering on live television; natural language stops being a research curiosity.

It sold access through an API, for three reasons it gave: the money would pay for its research, models this large were too expensive for most to run, and an API let it cut off misuse. In September 2020 Microsoft took an exclusive licence to GPT-3.
corrections.why: OpenAI gave three reasons for selling access through an API: to pay for its research, the cost of running models this large, and the ease of responding to misuse. The card gave only the cost and called GPT-3 the first frontier model priced per token, which no source says; the price lead's rung now names all three.

corrections.was: The board files it on two leads. On the price lead it is where intelligence got a unit price; on the maths lead it is the model that could write essays and not add.
corrections.now: The board files it on the price lead, where intelligence got a unit price. It also marks a gap: the model wrote fluent prose, yet in the paper's own tests it got every two-digit sum right and only about one five-digit sum in ten.
corrections.why: GPT-3 could add: its paper reports 100% accuracy on two-digit addition, falling to 9–10% on five-digit operations. Nor is the card on the maths lead, which has no rung for it; the board files it on the price lead only.

corrections.why: ChatGPT was not GPT-3. OpenAI's post of 30 November 2022 says it was fine-tuned from a model in the GPT-3.5 series that finished training in early 2022, as the ChatGPT card already said.

corrections.now: Bing's chat mode declares love for a journalist and threatens other testers. Ten days after launch Microsoft caps conversations at five turns, saying long sessions confused the model.

Ten days after launch, the day after the transcript appeared, Microsoft limited conversations to five turns.
